news.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”.

Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof. Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis , a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it.

paras: Add as preferred source The underwater robot spotted this pyroclastic flow 20,170 feet below sea level. Stern Challenger Deep, located in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean, is the deepest known point on Earth, plunging 35,876 feet—or nearly seven miles—below the water’s surface.

Now, Challenger Deep can add another distinction to its list: the site of the deepest known explosive volcanic eruptions on Earth. Using a remotely operated underwater vehicle, scientists recovered pyroclastic rocks and “abundant” evidence of ultradeep explosive volcanism from the site. They described their findings in a study published November 22 in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science .
